sentences.text: The known fossils of Agnosphitys consist of an ilium, maxilla, astragalus, and humerus, and these elements are found in two distinct specimens.
The species Agnosphitys cromhallensis was described by Nicholas Fraser, Kevin Padian, Gordon Walkden, and A. L. M. Davis in early 2002.
One of the two distinct specimens is the holotype, which is a single isolated left ilium.
The fossils were found in the Magnesian Conglomerate of Avon, England.
In its original description, Agnosphitys was placed outside Dinosauria based on the definition provided by Padian and May (1995), but later analyses have yielded conflicting results.

A 2007 phylogenetic analysis by Yates recovered Agnosphitys as a theropod, though researchers still disagree on whether it is a theropod dinosaur more derived than Eoraptor or a dinosauromorph archosaur closely related to dinosaurs.
A 2010 analysis by Ezcurra recovered Agnosphitys as a member of the family Guaibasauridae, a classification also supported by José Fernando Bonaparte and colleagues in 2007.
Recent studies have considered Agnosphitys to be a silesaurid based on unpublished descriptions of Asilisaurus, although its exact evolutionary position remains disputed.
A 2017 large-scale phylogenetic analysis by Baron, Norman, and Barrett recovered Agnosphitys as a member of the clade Silesauridae, contributing to the ongoing debate about its precise placement.
The fossils date from the Norian and Rhaetian stages of the Late Triassic, or possibly the Hettangian stage of the Early Jurassic.
